bugs: Second-precision timestamps: if an edit lands in the same second as the claim and after the job has read the rows, then updated_at == synced_at and the change is never resent. The window is very small, because the job normally runs seconds after the claim.
failed() clears sync_started_at on every id, without checking that the claim is still its own (app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:97-100). retryUntil makes this unlikely.
antipatterns: app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:29-36: the giveUpAt property is computed in the constructor, but Laravel already evaluates retryUntil() once at dispatch, so the property is redundant
tests/Feature/PushStockAllocationsTest.php:103-106: hand-rolled Mockery Job plus setJob() where withFakeQueueInteractions()/assertReleased() exists
app/Console/Commands/DispatchStockSync.php:23-28: lazyById(100)->pluck->chunk(100) and then values() re-chunks what chunkById already gives
database/migrations/...:20: the (disabled_at, synced_at) index does not match the readyToSync predicate well
strengths: The claim runs in a transaction with lockForUpdate and re-checks readyToSync, so it is safe even without onOneServer
synced_at = sync_started_at (the claim time), so edits made after the claim stay ready. The comment about MySQL's left-to-right assignment order is a real constraint worth keeping
The job only processes rows still claimed (whereNotNull sync_started_at), so a duplicate SQS delivery is a no-op and nothing is sent twice
A shared RateLimited middleware backed by a Redis limiter throttles proactively. A 429 also triggers a release that honours Retry-After, with a default and a cap
retryUntil stays inside the 15-minute claim window, and failed() releases claims so the next run picks the rows up
Thorough Pest tests with datasets covering the readiness matrix, 429 default/cap, 500 keeping the claim, failed(), and rows outside the batch being left alone

bugs: The job does not check that its rows are still claimed (app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:41-44). A duplicate SQS delivery, or a re-run, POSTs the same rows again; the probe saw 2 requests. This breaks 'sent exactly once per change', and the test 'can run twice without changing the outcome' hides it.

synced_at = $sentAt, captured just before the request (line 50). An edit in the same second, after the rows were read, leaves updated_at == synced_at, so the change is silently never resent. The probe confirmed this. The window is open on every request, not only right after a claim.

The claim relies on a second-precision equality check (where sync_started_at = $claimedAt, line 31-32) to know which rows it won. Two overlapping dispatchers in the same second would both think they own the rows. onOneServer mitigates this.
failed() clears sync_started_at unconditionally, even if the rows have since been reclaimed by another job (line 75-79).
antipatterns: app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:66: in_array inside partition is fine, but whereIn or a keyed lookup would be clearer
No proactive throttling across workers. It only reacts to 429s, so at 5,000 rows (50 jobs at once) every job hits the limit and burns attempts
strengths: Concise, modern code: the #[Scope], #[Fillable], #[Signature] and queue attributes, plus the scope's docblock explaining why toBase() is needed
chunkById with a conditional claim update that re-applies readyToSync
Handles 429 with release based on Retry-After and a cap. retryUntil is tied to the claim TTL, and failed() releases claims
The schedule uses onOneServer and withoutOverlapping(5)
Tests use withFakeQueueInteractions()->assertReleased, cover the in-flight edit with time travel, and simulate claim expiry with travel

v.rationale: impl-1 ranks first. Both test suites pass (impl-1: 37 tests, impl-2: 26). The two are close in style, and both use modern attributes, toBase() writes, retryUntil inside the claim window, and failed() releasing claims. impl-1 is better on the focus area. Its claim is transactional with a row lock, and the job only processes rows that are still claimed, so a duplicate SQS delivery sends nothing. My probe confirmed that impl-2 sends the same rows twice in that case. impl-1 also stamps synced_at with the claim time, which keeps edits made during the request ready to sync. impl-2 stamps the time just before the request, and my probe showed a same-second edit being lost. impl-1 also throttles through a shared Redis limiter, while impl-2 only reacts to 429s. impl-1 has some ceremony: a redundant giveUpAt property, Mockery instead of withFakeQueueInteractions, and lazyById plus chunk. These cost little next to impl-2's real exactly-once gaps.
